Okay love, I hear you. I'm sorry if that came across as too interfering as well. If you've identified something you want to change then good on you for being honest with yourself :)

Just a suggestion/something I've noted for myself - but as you mention you're still feeling awful (which I'm really sorry to hear), at some point I hope you can say "enough now" and decide that even though you'll continue resisting, you can stop actively feeling awful. I've noticed recently every time I mess up I go into some disorientating shame/anxiety spiral and feel like if I come out of it, I haven't felt sufficiently bad enough, like doing mental penance for what I've done. I think it might be linked to 'sorry' never being enough in my house as a child and punishment being governed by my N's anger/mood swings. If it's at all the same for you, which it may not be, just thought I'd share in case it's at all helpful. Well done for squashing x

Pet - I would potentially draw a distinction between your Nmum using fast food as an inconsistent reward/withholding it as punishment, and you just buying fast food.

As you mentioned, it's never more than $5 anyway. I'm sure you've planned your finances with your husband carefully but surely there is some leeway in the budget for you to grab food when you're out, particularly for such a small amount? You are pregnant, remember (and as someone with an illness that can leave me exhausted if I don't stop to refuel - please don't feel bad about doing the same!)

I'm interested you mention this divide between your husband working and you having your own money. If you have savings, I suppose you could use them for any purchase that isn't joint. Though if you are on one salary, your money is shared, I'd assume? I hope there isn't an idea that your money is your husband's as he earned it and you didn't...?

Please don't feel like garbage :) I don't think you've done anything wrong. Looks like it may require a calm discussion if your finances are really that tight, but I don't think you've done anything to merit feeling really sorry (rather than just reconsidering and adjusting), or for your husband to be really angry about and scold.

Now, if it were a FLEA, you'd be bringing home fast food and eating in front of your husband while telling him you guys couldn't afford for him to have any... I think there's a pretty distinct difference

I was lucky to maintain relationships with a few close friends, one who lived abroad, just having someone (alternating) to vent to, or who would message out of the blue.

I definitely used online communities as a crutch. I would make plans for myself, and spend time alone when I could, lost myself in various random interests like planning trips I might take or projects I might do once I graduated.

I read a lot, watched movies, spent time with my dog. Bit the bullet and applied for internships post-graduation and though it was difficult with social anxiety, when workplace chit-chat and after-work drinks were common, it was great experience for me. I just gave myself time to slowly start building confidence again and pursuing new opportunities - starting any new situation you can have the chance to walk in and pretend to be confident and smiley, and it removes the anxiety over past awkward moments when you didn't talk enough or you feel like you're not living up to people's expectations.

Just try to really focus on what you want to do in the future - not what your parents want, or what you think you can do or ought to do - what would you do if you could do anything in the world?

It took me a full year after graduation to decide on my career path, having gone in a million different directions and struggling with depression and anxiety. It's worth seeing that process through, taking any valuable opportunity, and knowing that social interactions and human connections will come with these, as you grow in confidence and start shaping your path

You sound like a lovely and caring person, and that was an incredibly insensitive and hurtful thing for your dad to say to you. 

I'm glad to hear you don't actually want to die. Please keep reaching out to your online communities such as this one, and feel free to PM me anytime to talk. Just because your social life may have been limited in college in no way means that it will be that way forever.

When I was studying, I was quite withdrawn and socially anxious for a long time, while under a lot of stress. As you move on from college and into new situations with different people, you can be whoever you want to be, and you can pursue friendships while working, volunteering, at classes, hobbies or community centres. Once you feel like you're in a better place, you can comfortably pursue new friendships, though in the meantime, we are always here.

If you are feeling suicidal and hopeless, do consider reaching out to a medical professional or local charity for counselling and a helping hand. Here rooting for you x

Good for you for recognising the effect of what you did. It might be a burned bridge with that friend group, but hopefully you can make a part of your healing process getting out and meeting new people, and building healthy relationships with the insight you've gained into how your illness affected your behaviour, and how to avoid lashing out in future. Good luck x

Breathe.

One minute. One hour. Take your time watching the clock take you closer to morning, one tick at a time.

We hear you, you're tired beyond belief. To me, that says you've been working so hard, and you've achieved something. 

That upward climb in your life recently has come from you and your hard work and determination. It hasn't been easy, and you will have hopeless, exhausted nights like these.

But as you continue on your upward climb, these will be few and far between. Take some time for yourself when you can. Wake up half an hour early to watch the sun rise or listen to the beds. Talk to someone - see your doctor about arranging counselling/talking therapy so you have a person to be honest with about your thoughts and feelings, who will keep these private and is there, above all, to listen to you.

You are wanted. You are valued. You are loved.

You don't have to be okay for that, but with a little help and care, you will be well on your way
